At the edge of a small town, where the streetlights gave up and the fields began, there stood a bench facing west.

Nobody knew who had put it there. It was not particularly beautiful: plain wood, iron legs, one board slightly warped by rain. In summer, ants traveled its length like commuters. In winter, frost gathered on it before dawn and made it shine blue in the early light.

People used it anyway.

A delivery driver sat there once after a difficult phone call, watching the sky turn orange behind the grain silos. An old woman brought a thermos of tea every Thursday and poured a second cup onto the ground for her husband, who had loved sunsets but had not lived long enough to see all the ones she wanted to show him. Teenagers came in pairs, pretending they had nowhere else to be. Children climbed on it and declared it a pirate ship, a train, a castle wall.

The bench asked nothing of them. It did not advise them, remember their names, or insist that they become better versions of themselves. It simply held their weight.

Years passed. The town grew by a few streets, then lost a factory, then gained a café with expensive pastries and plants in every window. Someone proposed removing the bench to make way for a paved walking trail. Someone else said it was rotten. Someone else said it was ugly.

But when the work crew arrived, the foreman found a small brass plaque beneath the seat, almost hidden by mud.

It read:

**FOR ANYONE WHO NEEDS TO STOP FOR A WHILE.**

So they built the trail around it.

And every evening, as the world continued doing its loud and urgent work, the bench remained at the edge of town, facing west—waiting patiently for the next person who needed to stop.
